case_analysis.focal_point: Whether False Claims Act scienter (“knowingly”) can be defeated by an after-the-fact, objectively reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous legal requirement (under Safeco), even if the defendant actually believed its claims were false when submitted.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729(a) and § 3729(b)(1) (definitions of “knowingly,” including actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (relators), supported by the United States and multiple amici, argue that FCA scienter is fundamentally subjective: liability turns on what the defendant actually knew or believed at the time it submitted claims. They contend the Seventh Circuit erred by importing Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework—developed in the Fair Credit Reporting Act context—to allow defendants to escape FCA liability based on a post hoc, lawyerly interpretation of an ambiguous requirement, even where evidence shows the defendant understood (or strongly suspected) its billing/price reporting was improper. In their view, the FCA’s text (“actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” “reckless disregard”) and anti-fraud purpose are undermined if a defendant can avoid liability merely by identifying some objectively reasonable reading not clearly foreclosed by authoritative guidance, regardless of its contemporaneous intent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that where alleged falsity depends on an ambiguous legal obligation, scienter should be assessed using the objective knowledge standard articulated in Safeco: a defendant does not act “knowingly” if it adopts an objectively reasonable interpretation and no authoritative guidance warned it away. They maintain that this approach properly protects regulated entities from punitive FCA exposure for reasonable interpretations of unclear rules, promotes fair notice, and aligns with the uniform approach of courts of appeals that have applied Safeco-like reasoning in FCA cases involving legal ambiguity. They also emphasize administrability and limiting FCA liability to clearly wrongful conduct rather than penalizing reasonable disagreement over uncertain legal standards.
key_precedents: Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point remains fair notice: where the legal duty is genuinely ambiguous and no authoritative guidance exists, treble damages can seem in tension with due-process values reflected in Safeco. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the FCA’s text expressly defines “knowingly” in three prongs keyed to the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state, and a post hoc “objectively reasonable” interpretation cannot categorically negate proof of actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance at submission. Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework construed “willfully” in a different statutory scheme and cannot be imported to rewrite § 3729(b)(1)(A) into an atextual safe harbor; at most, ambiguity is relevant evidence—especially on the recklessness prong and perhaps falsity/materiality at the margins. A narrow holding on those terms preserves institutional legitimacy by respecting Safeco’s context without displacing Congress’s chosen scienter structure here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that Safeco supplies an objective-reasonableness ceiling on “reckless disregard,” but the FCA’s text does not use an undifferentiated “willfully” standard; it enumerates three scienter prongs, including “actual knowledge,” which cannot be nullified by a post hoc legal theory. As Justice Gorsuch notes, importing Safeco here would effectively rewrite § 3729(b)(1)(A) into an atextual safe harbor even where the defendant contemporaneously believed the claim was false—precisely the conduct Congress captured in 1986. Justice Roberts’s narrower framing is also correct: ambiguity may be evidentiary on recklessness at the margins, but it is not a categorical defense that defeats proof of actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance at submission. Under an original public meaning approach, “knowingly” as Congress defined it focuses on the actor’s state of mind when presenting the claim, not on later lawyerly reconstructions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s fair-notice/Safeco argument has intuitive force, but it cannot overcome the FCA’s text: Congress defined “knowingly” in three distinct, subjective prongs keyed to what the defendant actually knew, deliberately avoided, or recklessly disregarded at the time of submission. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, a narrow rule suffices—legal ambiguity may be relevant evidence on recklessness, but an after-the-fact “objectively reasonable” interpretation cannot categorically negate proof of contemporaneous actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance without collapsing § 3729(b)(1)(A)(i)–(ii) into an objective test. Justice Thomas’s point about Safeco’s different statutory context reinforces the textual constraint: Safeco construed “willfully” without an enumerated scienter definition, so importing its safe harbor here would effectively rewrite the statute. Practical consequences also cut against respondent: allowing post hoc legal rationalizations to erase subjective bad faith would invite strategic ambiguity and materially weaken the FCA’s anti-fraud deterrent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent point is fair notice—if the underlying legal duty is genuinely ambiguous, defendants shouldn’t face treble damages for a reasonable interpretation—but the FCA answers that by requiring proof of what the defendant actually knew, deliberately ignored, or recklessly disregarded at submission, not by creating an atextual safe harbor. As Justice Kagan notes, ambiguity may be relevant evidence on recklessness, but it cannot categorically defeat scienter where there is proof of actual knowledge or deliberate avoidance; that approach respects both notice concerns and Congress’s tri-part definition in § 3729(b)(1)(A). Justice Roberts’s narrower framing is also persuasive: we need not repudiate Safeco wholesale; we can hold simply that Safeco’s objective-reasonableness concept for “willfully” in the FCRA does not erase contemporaneous subjective culpability under the FCA’s distinct text. Allowing post hoc lawyering to override evidence of what the defendant believed would drain the statute’s anti-fraud purpose and, in practical terms, reduce recoveries that fund programs serving vulnerable beneficiaries.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains Safeco’s fair-notice concern: ambiguity plus no authoritative guidance should not trigger punitive FCA liability. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3729(b)(1)(A) deliberately defines “knowingly” in contemporaneous, subjective terms—actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard—so a post hoc “objectively reasonable” legal theory cannot categorically defeat proof that the defendant in fact believed (or consciously avoided confirming) the claim’s falsity when submitted. Safeco’s objective-reasonableness approach, tailored to construing “willfully” in a different statute, can at most inform whether ambiguity makes it harder to prove recklessness on a given record; it cannot be transmuted into an atextual safe harbor that nullifies Congress’s separate actual-knowledge and deliberate-ignorance prongs. That narrower, text-centered rule also pragmatically preserves fair-notice values by letting ambiguity operate as evidence, without licensing after-the-fact lawyering to launder subjective bad faith.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is a fair-notice concern: that punishing regulated parties for taking a reasonable view of an ambiguous legal requirement risks turning the FCA into a trap for the unwary. But Congress answered that concern in the text by requiring proof the defendant acted with “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” or “reckless disregard,” § 3729(b)(1)(A), all of which are keyed to the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state, not a post hoc lawyerly justification. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, a narrow rule accommodates ambiguity as evidentiary context—especially for the recklessness prong—without creating an atextual safe harbor that would absolve defendants who in fact believed their claims were false. Safeco’s objective-reasonableness approach, focused on “willfully” in a different statute, cannot be imported to override Congress’s explicit, tripartite scienter definition here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains Safeco/fair-notice: treble damages should not attach when the legal duty is genuinely ambiguous and no authoritative guidance exists. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, Congress expressly defined “knowingly” in § 3729(b)(1)(A) in three prongs keyed to the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state, so a post hoc “objectively reasonable” interpretation cannot categorically negate proof of actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance at the time of submission. Justice Thomas’s textual point is decisive under an institutionalist approach: importing Safeco wholesale would effectively rewrite the statute into an atextual safe harbor and collapse distinct mens rea prongs Congress deliberately separated in 1986. Fair-notice concerns can be accommodated by treating ambiguity as relevant evidence—especially on the recklessness prong—without creating immunity where the factfinder concludes the defendant believed the claim was false.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains fair notice under Safeco: where the legal duty is genuinely ambiguous, treble-damages liability can seem unfair absent authoritative guidance. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FCA’s text defines “knowingly” in expressly subjective terms—actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard—so a post hoc “objectively reasonable” interpretation cannot categorically defeat proof that the defendant, at submission, believed the claim was false or consciously avoided confirming its falsity. Safeco construed “willfully” in a different statutory scheme lacking Congress’s tripartite mens rea definition here, and importing it wholesale would effectively rewrite § 3729(b)(1)(A) by collapsing distinct prongs into an atextual objective safe harbor. Ambiguity can still be relevant evidence on recklessness (and perhaps falsity/materiality), but it cannot erase contemporaneous subjective culpability the statute expressly targets.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s fair-notice/Safeco argument has real force where the underlying duty is genuinely uncertain, but it cannot justify an atextual categorical shield that overrides the FCA’s express focus on the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow approach is persuasive: ambiguity can be relevant evidence—especially on “reckless disregard”—yet it cannot erase proof that a defendant actually knew or deliberately avoided learning that its claims were false when submitted. Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch reinforce that Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework was tailored to a different statute and cannot be imported to collapse § 3729(b)(1)(A)’s three distinct scienter prongs into a post hoc “reasonable lawyer” defense. As a pragmatic matter tied to procedural fairness, allowing after-the-fact legal rationalizations to defeat scienter would systematically insulate intentional fraud and distort FCA enforcement away from Congress’s design.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FCA’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), which points to a defendant’s contemporaneous state of mind rather than an after-the-fact, objectively reasonable legal theory. Safeco construed “willfully” under the FCRA to allow an objective-reasonableness safe harbor absent authoritative guidance, 551 U.S. 47 (2007), but that framework does not fit where Congress expressly enumerated subjective scienter standards and where evidence may show the defendant believed its claims were false when submitted. A narrow ruling can resolve this case without rejecting all consideration of legal ambiguity: an objectively reasonable interpretation cannot defeat FCA scienter when the factfinder concludes the defendant actually knew, or was at least reckless to, the claim’s falsity at the time of submission. That approach hews to the statute’s plain language and preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding a broad reworking of Safeco beyond its context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The False Claims Act defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), and that text focuses on the defendant’s state of mind at the time it “presents” or “makes” a claim under § 3729(a), not a later-constructed legal justification. An after-the-fact, objectively reasonable interpretation cannot negate proof that the defendant actually believed its claims were false when submitted, because such evidence directly satisfies “actual knowledge” (and may also show “deliberate ignorance”) as those terms were commonly understood in fraud law and as Congress codified them in 1986. Safeco construed “willfully” in a different statute (the FCRA) and relied on fair-notice considerations tied to that term; it does not override the FCA’s more particular, enumerated scienter standard. Importing Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework would effectively rewrite § 3729(b)(1) and improperly create a quasi-qualified-immunity defense that the statutory text does not provide.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The False Claims Act’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), making scienter a state-of-mind inquiry focused on what the defendant believed when it submitted the claims. Safeco’s objective-reasonableness approach addressed when a defendant is “reckless” under a different statute and, even there, it did not purport to erase evidence of actual subjective knowledge; a defendant who actually believed its claims were false fits § 3729(b)(1)(A)(i) regardless of later-invented ambiguity arguments. Allowing an after-the-fact, lawyerly “reasonable interpretation” to defeat proof of actual knowledge would improperly collapse the statute’s three distinct scienter prongs into a single objective safe harbor and would invite fraud by rewarding willful blindness. Limiting liability for genuinely unclear obligations can be handled at the falsity/materiality stages, but where contemporaneous evidence shows the defendant thought it was violating the rule, the FCA’s text does not permit escape via post hoc reasonableness.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FCA’s text makes scienter a subjective inquiry keyed to what the defendant actually knew, deliberately ignored, or recklessly disregarded at the time of submission—31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A)(i)–(iii)—and it would be incoherent to let post hoc “objective reasonableness” erase evidence of actual knowledge. Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr construed “willfully” in the FCRA and used objective reasonableness largely to define “reckless disregard” in a statute lacking the FCA’s express, tripartite scienter definition; it does not license a rule that defeats FCA liability even where the defendant believed its claims were false. Allowing after-the-fact ambiguity arguments to trump contemporaneous intent would weaken the FCA’s anti-fraud purpose and diminish remedies that protect the public fisc and vulnerable beneficiaries of federal programs. Fair notice concerns can be addressed by requiring proof of subjective culpability under § 3729(b)(1), not by creating a categorical safe harbor untethered from what the defendant actually thought and did.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FCA’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1), all of which turn on the defendant’s state of mind at the time of submission; an after-the-fact “objectively reasonable” legal theory cannot negate evidence that the defendant actually believed its claims were false. Safeco construed “willfully” in the FCRA without a comparable, multi-pronged scienter definition and relied on an objective recklessness inquiry suited to that statutory context, not the fraud-focused scheme Congress adopted in the FCA. Extending Safeco here would be unworkable and undermine statutory coherence by letting intentional or suspected falsity escape liability whenever counsel can later articulate a plausible reading. The better middle-ground rule is that legal ambiguity may bear on whether the defendant was reckless, but it does not categorically defeat scienter where there is proof of actual knowledge or deliberate avoidance.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FCA’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), and that language directs attention to the defendant’s state of mind when submitting the claim—not to a later-constructed, objectively reasonable legal theory. Importing Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework would rewrite Congress’s chosen mens rea terms and effectively create an atextual safe harbor even for defendants who in fact believed their claims were false, contrary to ordinary principles that scienter turns on what the actor knew, suspected, or consciously ignored. At most, legal ambiguity is evidence bearing on whether a defendant was reckless or deliberately ignorant, but it cannot categorically defeat liability where the Government proves the defendant’s contemporaneous subjective belief of falsity. Nor does “no proof of specific intent to defraud” (§ 3729(b)(1)(B)) justify raising the bar by making even actual bad faith irrelevant.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FCA’s scienter definition is explicit and layered—“actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” or “reckless disregard” of falsity, 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A)—and those terms focus on the defendant’s contemporaneous state of mind, not a post hoc, lawyer-crafted theory of legality. Safeco construed “willfully” in the FCRA to include an objective-reasonableness safe harbor for recklessness, but it did not involve (and should not be extended to override) a statute that separately and expressly captures subjective culpability, including actual knowledge. As a practical and institutional matter, allowing an after-the-fact “reasonable interpretation” to defeat liability even when the defendant believed its claims were false would undercut the FCA’s fraud-deterrent design and invite gamesmanship; ambiguity may bear on whether the defendant was reckless, but it cannot negate proof of actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance at submission. Consistent with judicial restraint and the statutory text, scienter cannot be defeated where there is evidence the defendant actually believed the claims were false when presented.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FCA’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), which points to the defendant’s state of mind at the time the claim is submitted rather than a purely after-the-fact, objective inquiry. Safeco construed “willfully” in the Fair Credit Reporting Act and adopted an objective-reasonableness framework in that distinct statutory setting, but it did not involve (and cannot displace) Congress’s express, multi-pronged scienter definition in the FCA. Where evidence shows the defendant actually believed its claims were false when submitted, that fits comfortably within “actual knowledge” and is not negated by later identifying an arguable interpretation of an ambiguous requirement. Precedent may inform how “reckless disregard” is applied at the margins, but it cannot override the statute’s textual command that subjective knowledge is relevant to FCA scienter.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FCA expressly defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), which centers the defendant’s contemporaneous state of mind rather than a post hoc, lawyerly justification. Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework addressed “willfulness” in a different statutory setting and cannot override Congress’s text here—particularly where evidence shows the defendant actually believed the claims were false when submitted, which is the paradigmatic case of “actual knowledge.” Allowing an after-the-fact, objectively reasonable interpretation to negate scienter would undermine procedural fairness and the FCA’s anti-fraud purpose by insulating intentional wrongdoing whenever a regulation is later framed as ambiguous. At most, legal ambiguity may bear on whether a defendant was reckless, but it cannot defeat liability where the record supports actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance at the time of submission.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the False Claims Act’s scienter element (“knowingly”) is satisfied based on what the defendant actually believed and understood at the time of submitting claims, or whether a defendant can avoid liability by pointing to a post hoc “objectively reasonable” interpretation of an ambiguous legal requirement under Safeco.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1) (liability for false or fraudulent claims) and § 3729(b)(1) (definition of “knowingly” as actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (relators) argue that FCA scienter focuses on the defendant’s subjective state of mind when submitting claims: if the defendant actually knew its claims were false (or was deliberately ignorant or reckless), liability attaches even if clever lawyers can later construct an “objectively reasonable” reading of an ambiguous rule. They contend the Seventh Circuit wrongly imported Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework (developed in a different statute and context) to negate FCA knowledge, thereby allowing defendants who believed they were overcharging the government to escape liability so long as no controlling authority had expressly warned them off their interpretation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that when falsity depends on an ambiguous legal obligation, Safeco’s objective standard should govern scienter: a defendant does not act “knowingly” if it adopted an objectively reasonable interpretation of the law and no authoritative guidance made that interpretation untenable. They maintain this approach provides fair notice, prevents FCA liability from turning on hindsight about unclear rules, and aligns with the uniform approach of multiple circuits applying Safeco-like reasoning in FCA scienter disputes involving legal ambiguity.
key_precedents: Safeco Insurance Co. of America v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest opposing consideration remains Justice Alito’s fair-notice concern—if the law is genuinely ambiguous, it can seem harsh to brand a defendant “reckless” absent clear guidance. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, Congress answered that concern in the FCA’s text by defining “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge” and “deliberate ignorance,” which are inherently subjective and cannot be categorically defeated by a post hoc, objectively reasonable legal theory. Safeco is best read as context-bound—an effort to supply content to an undefined “willfully” in a different statutory regime—and it does not authorize us to graft an atextual safe harbor onto § 3729(b)(1). A narrow, legitimacy-preserving holding is that legal ambiguity is relevant evidence in assessing whether the Government proved knowledge/recklessness on these facts, but it is not a per se bar where the factfinder could find contemporaneous actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is fair notice: where a legal requirement is genuinely ambiguous and the defendant’s view is objectively reasonable absent authoritative guidance, calling the conduct “reckless” could seem to impose liability for unclear law. But the FCA’s enacted text forecloses converting that policy concern into a categorical safe harbor: Congress defined “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” and it expressly eliminated any “specific intent to defraud” requirement, § 3729(b)(1), directing the inquiry to the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state rather than post hoc lawyerly plausibility. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Safeco construed an undefined “willfully” term in a distinct statutory setting and cannot be imported to negate scienter even where evidence shows actual knowledge or deliberate avoidance. Ambiguity may be relevant evidence on what the defendant knew or disregarded, but it cannot, consistent with the statute’s original public meaning, categorically defeat liability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest Respondent argument remains fair notice: if the underlying legal duty is genuinely ambiguous, it seems harsh to brand a defendant “reckless” for adopting a plausible reading absent authoritative guidance. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan stress, Congress itself answered the scienter question in § 3729(b)(1) by expressly defining “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge” and “deliberate ignorance,” which cannot be nullified by a post hoc, objectively reasonable legal theory; Safeco, as the Chief notes, construed an undefined “willfully” in a distinct statutory scheme and does not supply a transsubstantive safe harbor here. The better textualist, consequence-aware approach is to treat ambiguity as powerful evidence that the Government cannot prove reckless disregard (or deliberate ignorance) on these facts, while rejecting any categorical rule that defeats scienter even where contemporaneous awareness or conscious avoidance is shown. That accommodates notice concerns without rewriting Congress’s calibrated mens rea definition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Respondent’s strongest point remains Justice Alito’s fair-notice concern drawn from Safeco—if the law is truly unclear, it seems harsh to label conduct “reckless.” But as the Chief and Justice Kagan explain, Safeco’s objective-reasonableness screen was a tool for an undefined “willfully” standard in a different statutory scheme; it cannot be imported to override the FCA’s express, tripartite scienter definition that turns on what the defendant actually knew, consciously avoided learning, or recklessly disregarded at the time. Genuine ambiguity can—and should—count as evidence that the Government failed to prove subjective culpability, yet it cannot become a categorical safe harbor that lets sophisticated actors escape liability through post hoc legal creativity even when internal facts show awareness of likely falsity. Keeping the focus on contemporaneous mindset best fits the statutory text and preserves the FCA’s practical role in protecting vulnerable beneficiaries from hidden overbilling.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest Respondent point remains Justice Alito’s fair-notice/Safeco concern, but the FCA’s text does the work here: § 3729(b)(1) expressly defines “knowingly” in subjective terms (“actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” “reckless disregard”), so a post hoc “objectively reasonable” legal theory cannot categorically negate scienter when the factfinder could find contemporaneous awareness or conscious avoidance. As the Chief (Justice Roberts) emphasizes, importing an objective safe harbor would make liability turn on later lawyering rather than the defendant’s real-time billing choices, undermining Congress’s three-pronged scheme and creating an unworkable enforcement rule. Fair notice is accommodated by treating genuine ambiguity as probative evidence that the Government has not carried its burden on recklessness (and by falsity/materiality constraints), not by rewriting the mens rea definition to require “authoritative guidance.” Safeco, as Justice Barrett notes, construed an undefined “willfully” in a different remedial setting and cannot displace Congress’s enacted FCA scienter standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest opposing consideration remains Justice Alito’s fair-notice/Safeco point, but as the Chief and Justice Kagan explain, Safeco’s objective-reasonableness screen was an interpretive move for an undefined “willfully” standard and cannot be transposed to override Congress’s express FCA definition of “knowingly.” Textually and as Justice Barrett stresses, § 3729(b)(1) directs the inquiry to the defendant’s contemporaneous mental state—actual knowledge and deliberate ignorance are necessarily subjective and are not negated by a later-cobbled “reasonable” legal theory. Fair-notice concerns are accommodated by treating genuine legal ambiguity as relevant evidence that may defeat proof of reckless disregard in a given case, not as a categorical safe harbor that nullifies proved subjective culpability. Separation-of-powers principles counsel applying the mens rea Congress enacted rather than adding an atextual “authoritative guidance” prerequisite to liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point is the fair-notice concern framed through Safeco’s objective-reasonableness approach, but as the Chief Justice notes, Safeco construed an undefined “willfully” in a different statutory scheme and cannot be used to add an atextual safe harbor that negates the FCA’s express three-pronged definition of “knowingly.” I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett that ambiguity can be powerful evidence that the Government has not carried its burden to prove reckless disregard (or deliberate ignorance) on these facts, but it cannot categorically defeat scienter where the factfinder finds contemporaneous awareness or conscious avoidance. Institutionally, a narrow rule hewing to § 3729(b)(1) preserves predictability and legitimacy by applying Congress’s chosen mens rea while still accommodating notice concerns through the ordinary proof inquiry into what the defendant actually knew and did at the time. Safeco remains relevant as context-bound guidance about “reckless” in civil-penalty settings, not as a transsubstantive override of a detailed scienter definition.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s fair-notice/Safeco argument is the strongest counter, but it fits poorly with the FCA’s expressly defined mens rea: “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard” are ordinary terms that turn on what this defendant knew, consciously avoided, or disregarded when it submitted the claim—not on a later-constructed, objectively reasonable legal theory. Safeco interpreted an undefined “willfully” in a different statutory setting and cannot be used to override Congress’s specific three-pronged definition in § 3729(b)(1) without effectively rewriting the statute to add an atextual safe harbor. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan note, ambiguity can be relevant evidence on whether the Government proves recklessness in the first instance, but it cannot categorically defeat scienter where the factfinder concludes the defendant actually knew (or deliberately avoided knowing) the truth or falsity at the time. On an originalist/textualist approach attentive to enacted language and the 1986 amendments’ design, the subjective inquiry is the better reading and preserves the statute’s calibrated scienter scheme.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the fair-notice concern: that imposing FCA liability for an “ambiguous” legal requirement could chill participation in federal programs absent authoritative guidance. But § 3729(b)(1) answers that concern through its mens rea calibration—liability turns on what the defendant actually knew, deliberately avoided learning, or recklessly disregarded when submitting claims, not on a post hoc “objectively reasonable” legal theory that may never have motivated the billing decision. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework arose from a different statutory term (“willfully”) in a distinct notice-centered context and cannot be used to categorically negate proof of actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance under the FCA’s express definition. Ambiguity remains relevant evidence on whether the Government can prove recklessness in the first instance, but it should not operate as a freestanding safe harbor that would undercut the statute’s practical anti-fraud function and procedural fairness to the Government and relators.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FCA’s text defines “knowingly” to include “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” and “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1), which naturally directs the inquiry to what the defendant understood and believed when it submitted the claim, not to a lawyerly post hoc construction. Safeco interpreted “willfully” in the FCRA to encompass recklessness and used an objective standard in a distinct notice-focused civil-penalty scheme, but it did not purport to rewrite express statutory scienter terms like “actual knowledge” or “deliberate ignorance.” Importing Safeco to allow an “objectively reasonable” interpretation to negate even proven subjective knowledge would narrow the FCA beyond its language and undercut Congress’s calibrated scienter requirement while still allowing defendants to contest falsity and materiality on narrow grounds. A minimal, legitimacy-preserving resolution is to hold that ambiguity may bear on whether the Government proves knowledge or recklessness in the first instance, but it cannot categorically defeat scienter where the factfinder finds the defendant actually knew, was deliberately ignorant, or acted in reckless disregard at the time of the claims.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The False Claims Act defines “knowingly” to mean “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” or “reckless disregard,” and it expressly dispenses with any requirement of “specific intent to defraud.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1). That text focuses on the defendant’s contemporaneous state of mind, not on whether lawyers can later craft an “objectively reasonable” interpretation of an ambiguous requirement to negate scienter. Importing Safeco’s post hoc objective-reasonableness rule would rewrite § 3729(b)(1) by substituting an external “fair notice” inquiry for the statute’s mens rea terms and would improperly create a safe harbor for those who subjectively believed their claims were false or acted in reckless disregard. Because the statutory language is clear, any contrary atextual gloss should be rejected even if some lower courts have extended Safeco beyond its context.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FCA defines “knowingly” to include “reckless disregard,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A), and Safeco held that “reckless” liability generally turns on an objective inquiry: whether the defendant ran an unjustifiably high risk of violating the law in light of the text and available guidance. 551 U.S. at 68–70. Where the alleged falsity depends on an ambiguous legal requirement and the defendant’s reading was objectively reasonable with no authoritative contrary notice, treating that conduct as “reckless” would expand the statute beyond fair notice and chill participation in federal programs with substantial practical costs. Although actual knowledge remains actionable under § 3729(b)(1)(A)(i), courts should not permit FCA liability to rest on hindsight about unclear legal obligations when the conduct fits within Safeco’s objective-reasonableness framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FCA’s text makes scienter turn on the defendant’s actual state of mind—“actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” or “reckless disregard”—not on a lawyered-up, post hoc “objectively reasonable” interpretation. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A). Importing Safeco’s objective-reasonableness safe harbor would improperly nullify Congress’s deliberate-ignorance and reckless-disregard prongs, which necessarily require attention to what the defendant understood and chose to ignore at the time of billing, and would undermine the FCA’s remedial purpose by allowing sophisticated actors to evade accountability despite contemporaneous awareness of likely falsity. Safeco’s discussion of “willfully” in a different statutory context cannot override the FCA’s express definition of “knowingly,” and fairness concerns about ambiguous rules are better handled through the statute’s mens rea elements as applied to the defendant’s contemporaneous beliefs and conduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FCA’s scienter element is defined by Congress in expressly subjective terms: a defendant acts “knowingly” when it has “actual knowledge,” “deliberate ignorance,” or “reckless disregard” of the truth or falsity of the claim, 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A). Importing Safeco’s post hoc “objectively reasonable interpretation” safe harbor would sit uneasily with that text, because reckless disregard turns on what the defendant did (or failed to do) to ascertain legality at the time, not on whether later lawyers can devise a plausible reading of ambiguity. Safeco construed an undefined “willfully” standard in the FCRA, 551 U.S. 47 (2007), and its objective framework cannot override the FCA’s more specific, fraud-adjacent statutory definition that Congress enacted to broaden—not narrow—liability beyond specific intent.
